blocks.text: Share the immutable part of many similar objects so it is stored once, and pass the varying part in from outside.

A flyweight splits state in two. **Intrinsic** state is identical across objects, immutable, and lives in a shared flyweight. **Extrinsic** state differs per use, so the caller keeps it and passes it in. A **factory** hands out one shared instance per distinct intrinsic value.

items: **Saves:** memory, when objects number in the millions and mostly repeat.
**Costs:** a lookup per creation and clumsier APIs.

blocks.text: Flyweight is a measured optimization, not a default. Profile first: on the JVM, a lighter data layout often saves more.

walkthrough.note: The flyweight holds only intrinsic state, here species and color. As a record it is immutable and has value equality, which the pool relies on.
The factory guarantees one canonical instance per value. `computeIfAbsent` makes creation atomic, so concurrent callers still share.
A `Tree` stores only extrinsic state (position) plus a reference to the shared type. Its `draw` passes the extrinsic values in.
Six trees are created from two species. Each asks the factory instead of calling `new TreeType`.
Only two flyweights exist, and trees 0 and 2 hold the very same object (`==` is true), while each tree still draws at its own position.

blocks.text: A time-series database ingesting millions of points per second.

Every point carries a metric name and a set of tags such as `host`, `region` and `service`, but there are only a few thousand distinct combinations. Storing the strings with each point would cost gigabytes. Each distinct combination becomes a shared immutable `SeriesKey`, interned on ingest, and a data point holds just the key reference, a timestamp and a value.

lines: record SeriesKey(String metric, Map<String, String> tags) {}
record Point(SeriesKey series, long ts, double value) {}

blocks.text: Payoff: memory scales with the number of distinct series, not with the number of points, and key comparison becomes an identity check.

lists.title: Use when
items: Millions of objects share a large, immutable part and a profile shows memory pressure.
Distinct intrinsic values are few compared with the object count.

lists.title: Avoid when
items: Most objects are unique, so there is little to share.
The shared part is small; the lookup costs more than it saves.

lists.title: Pitfalls
items: Mutable intrinsic state: one caller's change appears in every user.
A strong pool never releases entries; use weak references if the key space is open.
Extrinsic state threaded through every call makes APIs awkward.

lists.title: Overuse smells
items: Pooling tiny objects the JIT could scalar-replace.
A global static pool hidden in domain code.

lists.title: Modern Java
items: Records give immutable value types that suit flyweights.
String deduplication (`-XX:+UseStringDeduplication`) shares `String` backing arrays with no code changes.

rows.difference: A singleton is exactly one instance globally. Flyweight keeps one instance per distinct value, and many of them.
Immutable leaf nodes of a composite, such as glyphs in a document tree, are natural flyweights.
Sharing is only safe because flyweights are immutable: one change would leak to every holder. Immutable value objects are the natural material for a flyweight pool.
Prototype copies an object to avoid expensive construction. Flyweight avoids having many copies at all by sharing one.
A proxy stands in for one specific object, often to defer or guard access. A flyweight is shared among many users.

entries.name: Integer.valueOf
entries.detail: Caches boxed values from -128 to 127, so `valueOf(100) == valueOf(100)`; `Character.valueOf` caches 0 to 127.

entries.name: String.intern
entries.detail: Returns a canonical instance from the JVM string pool for each distinct character sequence.

entries.name: Interners.newWeakInterner
entries.detail: A pool of canonical instances held by weak references, so unused entries can be collected.

options.why: One immutable `Currency` per distinct code is shared by millions of `Price` objects, which hold only their own amount.
A singleton has one instance in total. Here there is one instance per distinct code.
There is a creation method, but its point is returning shared instances to save memory, not choosing a subclass.
Nothing is cloned; existing instances are looked up and reused.

exercises.scenario: A spreadsheet viewer loads sheets with five million cells. Each cell has a style (font, fill, borders) drawn from about forty distinct combinations, plus its own value and position. Memory is the bottleneck.

options.why: Forty immutable shared styles replace five million copies; value and position stay per cell.
Cloning a style per cell is exactly what multiplies memory here.
There are forty styles, not one, so a single shared instance cannot work.
Loading cells lazily defers cost, but each loaded cell would still carry its own style copy.

exercises.prompt: Explain Flyweight in your own words: what is intrinsic versus extrinsic state, and who creates the flyweights?

modelAnswer.text: Flyweight saves memory by sharing. Intrinsic state is identical across many objects and immutable, so it lives in one shared flyweight. Extrinsic state differs per use and is kept by the caller and passed in. A factory returns the existing flyweight for each distinct intrinsic value, so clients never call the constructor directly.

keyPoints: Intrinsic state is shared, immutable, and stored once
Extrinsic state is held by the caller and passed in
A factory pools instances per distinct value
It is a memory optimization; measure first
Not a singleton: many flyweights, one per value
